newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open firm before Greenspan testimony.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open firm before Greenspan testimony.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened slightly higher on Thursday as investors waited to hear what Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan would say in testimony before Congress later this morning.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 3/32 to 95-18/32, yielding 6.98 perent in early dealings. Two-year notes were unchanged at 99-12/32, yielding 6.22 percent.
Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan is scheduled to testify before Congress's Joint Economic Committee at 1000 EST/1500 GMT on monetary policy and interest rates.

Investors will listen to Greenspan's remarks to see whether the echo the hawkish tone of the first leg of his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony in February and whether they concur with numerous statements from various Fed officials asserting the need for a "pre-emptive" tactic to ward off inflation.
In advance of the mid-morning Greenspan testimony, the market gets a full plate of new economic data.

At 0830 EST/1330 GMT, January U.S. international trade figures are due. They are expected to show that the U.S. trade deficit widened just slightly in January to $10.7 billion from $10.29 billion in December.

Of continuing interest to the bond market are the level of new jobless claims for the latest week. These are expected to total 316,000, according to economists Reuters surveyed, up from a subdued level of 307,000 new claims for state unemployment insurance a week earlier. A claims level below 320,000 will be viewed as another piece of evidence that labor markets are tight and thus hold some potential for future wage and price pressures.
At 1000 EST/1500 GMT, the March Philadelphia Fed Survey, an index of business activity in the Philadelphia area, is expected to read 16.8 versus 17.4 in February.

"The early data -- particularly the jobless claims report -- will provide (the market) a trading opportunity, but Greenspan's testimony later in the morning will be the focus for the day" said David Shabelman, treasury market analyst at MMS International.

As far as technical boundaries go, Shabelman said a move over 108-23 in the June T-bond contract would be a positive, but the 108-07 level, corresponding to a 30-year cash bond yield of seven percent "still lurks."
"The focus in on Greenspan, more so than on the numbers," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.

"Since he spoke at the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, Greenspan's inflation outlook has proved correct but growth has been stronger than he outlined," said Stiles. "The first quarter is growing well above what he expected. So you have to be careful if he comments about being forward-looking and his assessment of what's driving the strength of the economy."
The Fed prefers the economy's strength to be led by investment spending rather than consumer spending.
Investment spending produces more capacity to grow and is not as inflationary as when it is led by exuberant consumer spending, said Stiles.
As far as jobless claims go, even 320,000 new claims would be a low number and still indicative of a tight labor market, said Stiles.

In early trade, the five-year note was up 1/32 at 98-21/32 to yield 6.57 percent. Ten-year notes were up 1/32 to 96-17/32 to yield 6.72 percent. At the short end of the maturity range, three-month bill rates were down one basis point to 5.14 percent. Six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.29 percent.
